ORCID

I study young massive star clusters and star-forming regions with X-ray telescopes, chiefly Chandra and XMM-Newton. My work centres on the hot plasma, massive stars and low-mass populations of Cygnus OB2 and Westerlund 1, and on statistical methods for low-count X-ray spectra. I am based at the Universidad Nacional de Río Negro, Sede Atlántica, in Viedma, Patagonia.

Active · since 2021

EWOCS: Westerlund 1 and 2

Core member of the Extended Westerlund One and Two Open Clusters Survey (Chandra and JWST), led from INAF – Palermo, in charge of the diffuse X-ray emission analysis. The survey studies the X-ray population, Wolf–Rayet stars and diffuse emission of the most massive young cluster in the Milky Way.

Mapping the hot gas that fills the Cygnus OB2 association and separating it from unresolved stars, using the Chandra Cygnus OB2 Legacy Survey.

MEGA-X campaign in the Carina Nebula

International ground- and satellite-based monitoring of the X-ray emitting massive stars of the Carina Nebula (X-MEGA). Optical spectroscopy of its targets revealed new massive O-type binaries and their orbits, and long-term monitoring followed the periodic events of η Carinae.

Seven of my papers, each told through one of its figures. X-ray telescopes see the Universe at its hottest: gas at millions of degrees, stellar flares and the shock waves of exploded stars. The colours in these images are not what the eye would see; they encode the energy of the X-ray photons.

2026 · Astronomy & Astrophysics · First author

The hot breath of a super star cluster

EWOCS-VII: Unveiling the faint diffuse X-ray emission in Westerlund 1

Westerlund 1 is the closest super star cluster to the Sun, home to more than 100,000 stars. Its most massive stars blow winds so powerful that, when they collide, they heat the gas between the stars to tens of millions of degrees. After carefully removing almost five thousand individual stars from the deep Chandra images of the EWOCS survey, we could map this faint glow for the first time. In the core it comes from colliding winds of Wolf–Rayet stars; further out, the hot gas touches cold clouds and exchanges electrons with them.

Chandra observations
36
Stars removed
4,922
Gas temperature
21–48 MK

2023 · ApJ Supplement · First author

A stellar nursery wrapped in million-degree gas

Diffuse X-ray emission in the Cygnus OB2 association

Cygnus OB2 is one of the largest groups of massive stars in our Galaxy. Using 40 Chandra pointings that cover an area five times the full Moon, we removed nearly eight thousand stars to reveal the gas between them. That gas fills the whole region, heated by stellar winds that crash into each other and into the surrounding clouds. We also found the first signs of X-ray halos around some evolved massive stars.

2023 · ApJ Supplement · First author

How much can a handful of photons tell us?

The statistical uncertainties on X-ray flux and spectral parameters from Chandra ACIS-I observations of faint sources

Most young stars in a distant cluster send us only a few dozen X-ray photons during an observation. How well can we measure their temperature or brightness from so little light? We simulated 150,000 artificial spectra to find out, and built maps that give the error bars directly. They let astronomers know how far they can trust a measurement before they even fit the data.

2012 · Astrophysics and Space Science · Co-author

The glowing remains of an exploded star

A multiwavelength study of the supernova remnant G296.8-0.3

When a massive star explodes, its shock wave heats the surrounding gas for thousands of years. Combining X-ray, radio and infrared images, we showed that this remnant lies at least 29,000 light-years away and contains gas at about 10 million degrees. Near its centre we found a point-like X-ray source that may be the neutron star left behind by the explosion.

Distance
> 9 kpc
Gas temperature
≈ 10 MK
Telescope

2008 · Astronomy & Astrophysics · First author

A thousand young suns in the Carina Nebula

An X-ray survey of low-mass stars in Trumpler 16 with Chandra

Young stars like the early Sun are much brighter in X-rays than they are today, so X-ray images find them even inside dusty nebulae. In Trumpler 16, a 3-million-year-old cluster next to the giant star η Carinae, we detected over a thousand X-ray sources. Many of their planet-forming disks have survived the harsh light of their massive neighbours.

Stars with disks

Read the paper · A&A 490, 1055

2007 · Astronomy & Astrophysics · First author

Stellar storms in young stars

X-ray flaring from the young stars in Cygnus OB2

Young stars are magnetically violent: their flares are far more powerful than those of today's Sun. We catalogued the flares of about a thousand young stars in Cygnus OB2 and compared them with stars in the Orion Nebula. Stars of 1 and 2 million years flare in the same way, which tells us this activity changes slowly in a star's youth.

Read the paper · A&A 474, 495

2003 · Monthly Notices of the RAS · First author

The Carina Nebula through X-ray eyes

XMM-Newton X-ray observations of the Carina nebula

The Carina Nebula hosts some of the most massive stars known, including η Carinae. Using the European XMM-Newton satellite, we catalogued its X-ray sources and measured how the X-ray brightness of massive stars follows their total light. Some stars turned out to be surprisingly bright at high energies, a sign of colliding winds in binary systems.

Monitoring time

    The Café Científico series, talks for general audiences about stars and the Universe, and scientific presentations at conferences, seminars and universities.

    Café Científico 11

    An outreach series at Sol de la Ribera: a talk, questions and conversation about the Universe, over a coffee or a beer.

    13 October 2026 · Café Científico II, Part II · Sol de la Ribera · Tuesday · in Spanish

    Agujeros negros y la muerte del Universo · Parte II

    The second part of the black-hole evening. Anatomy of a black hole and the images of M87* and Sgr A* from the Event Horizon Telescope; quantum fluctuations, Hawking radiation and the information paradox, from the Page curve to the 2019 entanglement islands; GW250114, the 2025 gravitational-wave event that confirmed Hawking's area theorem; DESI's hints of evolving dark energy; and the possible fates of the Universe, down to the last black holes evaporating after 10¹⁰⁰ years.

    View the slides

    9 June 2026 · Café Científico XIII · Sol de la Ribera · Tuesday, 9 pm · in Spanish

    El final del tiempo · Parte I

    What is time? From Aristotle's measure of change and Newton's absolute time to Einstein's spacetime, light cones and the end of absolute simultaneity. Why time only runs forward (entropy and Boltzmann's S = k log Ω), the role of time in quantum physics, the energy–time uncertainty relation, and the Wheeler–DeWitt equation, in which time disappears altogether.

    View the slides

    17 March 2026 · Café Científico XI · Sol de la Ribera · Tuesday, 9 pm · in Spanish

    Vida extraterrestre vs. inteligencia extraterrestre

    What is life, and why C-H-O-N-S-P and water are everywhere in the Universe. Habitable zones around stars and in the Galaxy, the Drake and Seager equations, the famous Wow! signal and SETI, and the JWST hints of possible biosignatures in the atmosphere of the exoplanet K2-18 b. Life elsewhere versus intelligent life elsewhere: two very different questions.

    View the slides

    10 February 2026 · Café Científico X · Sol de la Ribera · Tuesday, 9 pm · in Spanish

    El destino del Universo · Pistas de una teoría incompleta

    How will the Universe end? What today's cosmology suggests about its ultimate fate, and why those clues point to an incomplete theory, where quantum field theory comes in and the very nature of spacetime is up for debate.

    View the slides

    6 November 2025 · Café Científico VIII · Sol de la Ribera · Thursday, 9 pm · in Spanish

    Visitantes de otros mundos · 3I/ATLAS, ¿nave extraterrestre?

    From conspiracy to the scientific method. The three interstellar objects detected so far: 1I/ʻOumuamua (2017) and its puzzling acceleration, 2I/Borisov (2019) and its CO and HCN, and 3I/ATLAS, with its hyperbolic orbit at ~68 km/s, its light curve, a coma dominated by CO₂ (JWST), nickel and iron, the green glow and what its composition says about its age. How the alien-spacecraft myth was born, and what we still have to wait for.

    View the slides

    8 October 2025 · Café Científico VII · Sol de la Ribera · Wednesday, 9 pm · in Spanish

    Agujeros negros observables

    What we can actually observe of black holes: Sagittarius A*, the four-million-solar-mass black hole at the centre of our Galaxy (2020 Nobel Prize to Penrose, Genzel and Ghez), and the first image of the supermassive black hole in M87. Primordial black holes, quantum entanglement, Hawking radiation and the information paradox, and ultramassive giants such as TON 618.

    View the slides

    3 September 2025 · Café Científico VI · Sol de la Ribera · Wednesday, 8:30 pm · in Spanish

    Big Bang · ¿Origen del Universo?

    From Olbers' paradox to the expanding Universe: Hubble's law and cosmological redshift, Lemaître's primeval atom, the cosmic microwave background and the tiny fluctuations measured by Planck that seeded the galaxies. What we know about the Big Bang, and what remains an open question.

    View the slides

    25 June 2025 · Café Científico IV · Sol de la Ribera · Wednesday, 8:30 pm · in Spanish

    Ondas gravitacionales · y colisión de agujeros negros

    What is gravity? From Newton's action at a distance to Einstein's spacetime and the waves it predicted but doubted. The Hulse–Taylor pulsar, Weber's bars, and how LIGO measures changes of 10⁻²¹ metres: the first detection, GW150914 (two black holes of 36 and 29 solar masses), and the neutron-star merger GW170817, a kilonova that forged gold. What comes next: NANOGrav and LISA.

    View the slides

    23 May 2025 · Café Científico III · Sol de la Ribera · Friday, 8:30 pm · in Spanish

    Objetos del Universo · ¿Qué ves cuando mirás?

    A tour of what we see when we look up: the Sun, planets, moons and asteroids. Kepler, Brahe and planetary orbits, protoplanetary discs, planetary migration (the Nice model and Jupiter's Grand Tack, with Saturn to the rescue), and the moons of the Solar System, from the Galilean moons to Titan, Enceladus and the Cassini mission.

    View the slides

    25 April 2025 · Café Científico II · Sol de la Ribera · Friday, 8 pm · in Spanish

    Agujeros negros y la muerte del Universo

    From Michell and Laplace's dark stars to Einstein's curved spacetime: the equivalence principle, time dilation and light bending. Primordial and supermassive black holes (M87, TON 618), quantum vacuum fluctuations and entanglement, Hawking radiation and the information paradox — and a Universe of black holes slowly evaporating over 10¹⁰⁰ years.

    View the slides

    2025 · Café Científico I · Sol de la Ribera · the first of the series · in Spanish

    Nacimiento, vida y muerte de las estrellas

    The opening talk of the series. How molecular clouds collapse into protostars (Hubble and JWST images), the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, why stars shine (Bethe, Einstein, the proton–proton chain and the CNO cycle), the eternal struggle between gravity and radiation, supernovae and neutrinos, Betelgeuse as a latent threat, and how every element we are made of was forged in stars. It closes with the story behind the novel El presagio de los neutrinos.

    Science fiction · for all ages

    El presagio de los Neutrinos

    What would happen if a star exploded as a supernova close to the Earth? Long before its light arrived, a burst of neutrinos would announce it. My novel follows that warning and imagines what it would mean for us. It draws on the science of massive stars, whose final moments matter most for life in the Universe.

    Living on the Río Negro, a few kilometres from the Atlantic, shapes much of what I do outside research: the water, the dark Patagonian sky and long journeys south and west.

    Swimming

    Open water

    Co-director of the Asociación Civil y Deportiva Open Water in Viedma, which organises open water competitions on the Río Negro, and one of the coaches of the swimming programme at Club Sol de Mayo.

    Photography

    Landscapes and night skies

    Photographing Patagonian and Andean landscapes, and the dark skies that make the region a natural observatory.

    Travel

    Patagonia and the Andes

    Journeys to remote and extreme landscapes in the south and along the cordillera, with an eye on the 2027 annular solar eclipse over Patagonia.
